breaking.headline: Nvidia board rejects Huang’s return as earnings beat big
breaking.fact: Jensen Huang said Tuesday he would be “honored” to return as Nvidia CEO, five days after resigning over extramarital affairs including one with a woman U.S. officials suspect was recruited by Chinese intelligence. Hours later, board chair Harvey Jones opened the earnings call by saying the board unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation and does not intend to reinstate him, and that the permanent-CEO search continues under interim CEO Colette Kress. Huang has agreed to closed-door testimony before three House committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia reported fiscal Q3 revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% year over year, with adjusted EPS of $2.68 against $2.47 expected, and guided Q4 revenue to $130 billion; shares rose nearly 4% after hours.

breaking.headline: Trump lands in China as Xi and Putin greet him; three-way talks Thursday
breaking.fact: President Trump landed in Shenzhen on Wednesday, where Xi Jinping greeted him on the tarmac — believed to be the first time Xi has personally greeted an arriving leader — and Trump shook hands with Vladimir Putin ahead of Thursday’s first-ever three-way meeting of the U.S., Chinese and Russian leaders at the APEC summit. Trump left the Philippines claiming a “very big trade deal” without giving details.

breaking.headline: Anthropic set to price IPO tonight, likely above $80 a share
breaking.fact: The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that Anthropic expects to price its IPO above its $70–$78 range, at more than $80 a share, after orders ran about six to seven times the 825 million shares on offer — a price that would value the Claude maker at roughly $1.5–$1.6 trillion. Final pricing is expected Wednesday evening, with trading to begin Thursday on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, alongside a $26 billion private placement from Google, Nvidia, Microsoft and other strategic partners.

breaking.headline: Peltola wins Alaska, giving Democrats a 56–44 Senate majority
breaking.fact: The Associated Press called Alaska’s Senate race for Democrat Mary Peltola on Tuesday night, the last undecided Senate contest in the country, after all 401 precincts reported. Peltola took 50.12% of first-choice votes to Sen. Dan Sullivan’s 45.80%, winning outright under Alaska’s ranked-choice system without elimination rounds. She becomes the first Alaska Native elected to the Senate, and her win — the ninth Democratic flip of the midterms — gives the party a 56–44 majority, its largest since 2009.

weekInBrief.headline: Fed minutes due at 2 p.m. ET as a December hike is nearly fully priced
weekInBrief.body: Minutes of the Fed’s Oct. 27–28 meeting arrive at 2 p.m. ET Wednesday; the Fed held its target range at 3.75%–4.00% on a 10–2 vote, with Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack dissenting in favor of a hike. Traders now price a 25-basis-point December hike at roughly 92%–96%, with Governor Christopher Waller floating 50 basis points, and the 10-year Treasury yield sits at 5.10%.

weekInBrief.headline: Congo Ebola outbreak passes 11,000 cases, still not under control
weekInBrief.body: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has passed 11,000 cases and 5,500 deaths since it was declared May 15, the second-largest outbreak on record, and Africa CDC says it is still not under control six months on. The WHO says 400–500 new cases are still reported each week, with children paying a terrible price — more than a quarter of confirmed cases — and cases have spread beyond the DRC to Kenya and Nigeria.

weekInBrief.headline: El Niño-driven waves batter California coast as atmospheric rivers arrive
weekInBrief.body: Waves topped 30 feet along the California coast, with a NOAA buoy off Monterey recording a 34.1-foot wave — its highest in 30 years — and waves above 50 feet reported in San Mateo County on Saturday. Forecasters warn of more dangerous surf and two storms this week, with flood risk from the Bay Area to San Diego, heavy Sierra snow and Thanksgiving travel disruption, as a strong El Niño keeps aiming atmospheric rivers at the West Coast.

weekInBrief.headline: U.S. loses measles elimination status after 26 years
weekInBrief.body: The Pan American Health Organization announced Tuesday that the United States has lost its measles elimination status, held since 2000, after the virus circulated uninterrupted for more than a year. The CDC has confirmed 5,412 measles cases in 2026 — the highest annual total since 1991 — with 96% of cases in people unvaccinated or of unknown status; Mexico and Bolivia lost their status too.

items.headline: Latest from the Strait
items.body: U.S. jets struck an IRGC missile site on Qeshm Island on Tuesday, answering Iranian drone attacks on a U.S. radar at Bahrain’s Sheikh Isa air base; overnight, Iran hit back with drones at Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem air base, which hosts U.S. forces, and at Bahrain for a fourth time in six days, with air defenses in both countries reporting interceptions and Tehran claiming hits on Patriot batteries. An ADNOC Logistics & Services vessel was attacked in the strait on Tuesday evening, leaving one crew member missing and 11 injured, and the LPG carrier Tara Gas caught fire off Oman’s Musandam peninsula after being struck; Iran’s state media now claims six tankers caught fire after striking naval mines in the past 48 hours, a claim no independent source has verified, and Iraq resumed pumping oil through its pipeline to Turkey to bypass the strait. On oil, the blockade still holds — UANI’s Nov. 16 update says no Iranian crude tanker has evaded it since July 14, while flows through the strait itself averaged about 8.6 million barrels a day in the week to Nov. 17, down from about 13.5 million in early November, per the independent Hormuz Strait Tracker, and Kpler puts total Gulf exports at about 11 million barrels a day as of Nov. 16.

space.headline: Musk unveils a much bigger Starship V4: 70 metres, nine engines, 200-ton payload
space.body: Elon Musk posted Nov. 15–16 that Starship V4’s upper stage will be about 70 metres long — roughly 40% longer than the current ship — carrying more than 60% more propellant, with nine higher-thrust Raptor engines, three more Raptor Vacuums. He projects propellant cost below $500,000 per flight and payload above 200 tons, with a first flight targeted in 2027; it follows Flight 15’s first-ever tower catch of Ship 42, which Musk says could fly again after weeks of refurbishment, while SpaceX still investigates why Booster 22’s catch aborted.

space.headline: Voyager 1 crosses one light-day from Earth
space.body: At 5:16 a.m. ET today, NASA’s Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to sit one full light-day — about 16.1 billion miles — from Earth, 49 years, two months and 11 days after launch. Radio signals now take a full day to reach it and another day to return; NASA marked the night with its “Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day” event, asking people to flash V-G-R in Morse code skyward, and holds a JPL panel Thursday. Voyager 2, travelling more slowly, will not reach the mark until 2035.

space.headline: Genetic ‘dimmer switch’ boosts sepsis resistance
space.body: UC Santa Cruz researchers found that a long noncoding RNA called Gaplinc acts as a genetic dimmer switch in macrophages, swaying whether the body survives severe, life-threatening inflammation; mice with higher Gaplinc levels survived endotoxic shock better. The work, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, points to a new strategy for treating sepsis, which kills at least 20% of adults who develop it, according to the CDC.

space.headline: A toxin helps African lungfish survive on land
space.body: University of New Mexico researchers found that African lungfish use a naturally occurring pore-forming toxin to remodel their skin from an aquatic to a terrestrial configuration as droughts drive them onto land each year. The discovery, published in the journal Cell, reveals how a toxin was evolutionarily repurposed to drive the epithelial remodeling behind the lungfish’s move from water to land.

apod.title: A Medium-Sized Solar Flare
apod.credit: Mario Cogo — NASA Astronomy Picture of the Day, November 18, 2026
apod.explanation: What a flare for the chromatic! Today’s image captures a piece of the Sun’s chromosphere, the layer of the Sun’s atmosphere above its surface where the temperature rises. Why would the Sun become hotter farther away from its core? This is potentially due to energy from the swirling magnetic fields extending up through the Sun’s atmosphere. Those same magnetic fields can twist and snap, releasing light and energetic particles as a solar flare. The H-alpha filter used for today’s image captures light from energized hydrogen atoms as they travel off the Sun’s surface during a flare on May 14, 2025. This flare was classified as an M1 based on GOES observations, meaning it was moderately bright in X-rays. M-class flares can cause radio blackouts at Earth’s poles and minor radiation storms that can harm astronauts. They aren’t even the most powerful flares! NASA, NOAA, and other agencies monitor the Sun to predict and identify such storms so we can protect humans on Earth and in space.
